candidates.attacker_control: Attacker controls YAML text/bytes that a consuming application passes to the library's public parsing entry points: Yaml.load(String/File/Reader), Yaml.loadAs(String/File/Reader, Class), Yaml.loadAll(String/File/Reader), Yaml.dump (not a sink), or Dynamics.newFromYaml / fromYamlToJson (e.g. a multi-tenant 'apply user-supplied manifest', templating, CI or log-processing service that parses untrusted YAML). No sanitization occurs between the input and SnakeYAML's constructor.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for safer parsing elsewhere: KubeConfig.java:83 uses `new Yaml(new SafeConstructor())` for kubeconfig, proving the codebase knows the mitigation but does not apply it to the manifest APIs; FilePersister.java:53 uses `new Yaml()` only for dump (serialization), which is not this sink. Checked in-repo callers: the spring manifest processors and examples parse classpath/local files (trusted), so the issue is only reachable when a consuming application feeds untrusted YAML to these public APIs (library-dangerous-default, not reachable from repo code alone). Also checked for tag filtering/whitelisting in Yaml.java - none; `CustomConstructor` overrides only type mapping for IntOrString/byte[]/OffsetDateTime and delegates everything else to the unrestricted Constructor. No CVE/GHSA/CWE annotation exists in the repo that would show an intended 'trusted input only' contract.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the JVM that parses the YAML (process memory, mounted service-account tokens/client keys read by the library, outbound network access), i.e. full compromise of the client/controller process if it accepts YAML from an attacker. Lower-end impact includes class-loading side effects and denial of service via crafted tags/aliases.
candidates.prerequisites: A consuming application parses YAML from a less-trusted source with these APIs; the JVM classpath contains at least one usable deserialization gadget for the `!!` tag path (the canonical SnakeYAML payload uses javax.script.ScriptEngineManager with a java.net.URLClassLoader to load a remote JAR, i.e. requires an outbound connection; other classpath-dependent gadgets also apply); snakeyaml is 1.x (<2.0), which this snapshot pins at 1.28.
candidates.root_cause: io.kubernetes.client.util.Yaml binds YAML to Kubernetes models through `CustomConstructor extends org.yaml.snakeyaml.constructor.Constructor` (Yaml.java:219-234) and exposes it via `getSnakeYaml()` -> `new org.yaml.snakeyaml.Yaml(new CustomConstructor(), new CustomRepresenter())` (Yaml.java:359-362). `Constructor`/its subclasses honor YAML global tags and instantiate arbitrary classes via Class.forName + bean property/constructor handling; snakeyaml 1.28 (pom.xml:43, dependencyManagement pom.xml:100-104, used in util/pom.xml:33-36) predates the 2.0 default restriction. `io.kubernetes.client.util.generic.dynamic.Dynamics` is worse and uses the raw unsafe default `new Yaml()` (Dynamics.java:24) and calls `yamlCodec.load(yamlContent)` (Dynamics.java:62-64). There is no tag whitelist, no SafeConstructor/TrustedPrefixes filtering and no documented 'trusted input only' contract on these public APIs, so YAML-level tags (`!!...`) reach class loading/instantiation in the client JVM.
candidates.title: Unsafe SnakeYAML deserialization in Yaml/Dynamics YAML parsing APIs (snakeyaml 1.28, non-safe Constructor)
candidates.trace: Untrusted YAML string -> Yaml.load(content)/load(new File)/load(Reader) (Yaml.java:58-83) or loadAs (94-120) or loadAll (133-176), or Dynamics.newFromYaml/fromYamlToJson (Dynamics.java:44-65) -> getSnakeYaml()/internalYamlCodec = new Yaml(...) (Yaml.java:360-362, Dynamics.java:24) -> SnakeYAML Constructor.getConstructor/constructObject (CustomConstructor.constructObject calls super.constructObject at Yaml.java:233, Dynamics uses the stock unsafe Constructor) -> tag-directed Class.forName/instantiation in the client JVM -> attacker-controlled code execution/data exfiltration on the host running the client. KubeConfig.loadKubeConfig (KubeConfig.java:83) demonstrates the safe alternative in the same codebase.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified (no code executed; build/tests not run). Exact gadget availability depends on the consuming application's classpath, and exploitability depends on that application treating YAML content as untrusted. I could not verify the precise SnakeYAML 1.28 class-filtering behavior from source in this snapshot (dependency jar not present); the assessment relies on the documented CVE-2022-1471 behavior of Constructor/`new Yaml()` before snakeyaml 2.0. Could not inspect the 7 name-filtered files in util/.../util/credentials/ or binary/>5MiB excluded files.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (unsafe SnakeYAML Constructor; CVE-2022-1471 class)

coverage_summary: Model-visible coverage: 2198/2208 source files (3 excluded as >5MiB, 7 excluded by sensitive name/path, 0 symlinks). P1 relation index reports 2208/2208 files indexed, 116,815 symbols and 195,434 edges, with no SAST/findings oracle loaded. I inspected the hand-written security-relevant code in util (KubeConfig, ClientBuilder, Config, SSLUtils, Yaml, Dynamics, Copy, Exec, Attach, PortForward, PodLogs, Watch/WebSockets/WebSocketStreamHandler, PatchUtils, Streams, Preconditions, informer/controller helpers, generic API, caveat: all 7 files in util/.../util/credentials/ are excluded from the visible source and could not be read), extended (kubectl commands, controller/leader-election/network/pager), spring (reconciler, informer factory, manifest processors/autoconfig), and the hand-written classes inside the kubernetes module (JSON, ApiClient TLS/SSL settings, auth, custom Quantity/IntOrString), plus POM dependency versions, CI workflows and dev scripts. The kubernetes/proto/client-java-contrib model/API classes are machine-generated and were sampled rather than exhaustively read; four duplicated examples-release trees (10-13) were spot-checked. No build, tests, scanners or code were executed; no runtime confirmation is claimed.
limitations: No code execution, build, tests or scanners were run; all findings are static source evidence only and are unverified at runtime.

The 7 files under util/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/util/credentials/ (Authentication implementations, KubeconfigAuthentication, ClientCertificateAuthentication, TokenFileAuthentication, AccessTokenAuthentication, UsernamePasswordAuthentication, etc.) are filtered out of the visible source view; their behaviour could change the impact analysis of several leads (e.g. how a null client certificate is handled).
3 binary/>5MiB files are excluded and binary-like files are refused by read_file, so those contents were not reviewed.
The kubernetes module's generated ApiClient/apis/models (and proto/client-java-contrib generated code) were only sampled; a modification hidden in generated code would likely be missed.
No tests or e2e sources are present in the snapshot (e.g. e2e only has pom.xml), so intended behaviour could not be cross-checked against tests.
The P1 index is navigational only (no data-flow, reachability or exploitability proof); index categories such as 'process'/'deserialization' are name-based hints and were not treated as findings.

Assumption of untrusted YAML is application-dependent; the repository's own in-tree callers parse local/classpath YAML, so this candidate is a dangerous library default rather than a demonstrated in-repo exploit.

rejected_leads.lead: Shell command injection in util/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/Copy.java: srcPath/parentPath are concatenated into `sh -c` strings (lines 87, 179, 296, 420) with no quoting.
rejected_leads.reason: Real CWE-78-style concatenation, but the command executes inside the target container (not on the client host), the path is normally supplied by the tool operator/caller, and this matches upstream's intended kubectl-cp-like design; impact is largely equivalent to the exec capability the caller already holds. Kept as a plausible secondary lead, not the top candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Kubeconfig persistence with default file permissions in util/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/util/FilePersister.java:52-56 (FileWriter, no 0600/ACL, in-place truncation, symlink-following).
rejected_leads.reason: Kubeconfigs can contain tokens/client keys (credential disclosure to local users/other containers), but exploitation requires local access to the file path, and the code comment at line 50 acknowledges the limitation; no attacker-controlled input boundary in the library itself.

rejected_leads.lead: KubectlPortForward binds `new ServerSocket(localPort)` (extended/.../KubectlPortForward.java:83) to the wildcard address, exposing forwarded pod ports to the network (kubectl defaults to loopback).
rejected_leads.reason: Security-relevant exposure, but the same wildcard bind is used in the repo's own PortForwardExample (line 50), so it appears to be intended upstream behaviour rather than a defect introduced here; impact depends on what the caller forwards.

rejected_leads.lead: CSRUtils.waitUntilCertificateSigned lambda returns true unconditionally after a successful CSR read (util/.../CSRUtils.java:172-184), so it can return a null certificate and report success before the CSR is signed/approved.
rejected_leads.reason: Internally inconsistent logic (ifPresent-set then unconditional return) and a real bug, but the observable impact is a null certificate / failed authentication (DoS/correctness) rather than an auth bypass; could not confirm it against upstream and could not inspect ClientCertificateAuthentication (credentials package excluded from the visible source view).

rejected_leads.lead: WebSocketStreamHandler.write(byte[],int,int) tracks `remaining -= bytesWritten` instead of the chunk size (util/.../WebSocketStreamHandler.java:261-274), producing a negative buffer size on writes > ~30MiB (NegativeArraySizeException).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible injected-looking off-by-design, but the security impact is limited to a failed large copy/DoS of the calling thread; no attacker-controlled server-side boundary established.

rejected_leads.lead: Attach.ConnectionBuilder only defaults stdin=true (util/.../Attach.java:153-157), leaving stdout/stderr false although AttachResult exposes stdout/stderr streams and the shipped AttachExample reads stdout.
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like a functional regression rather than a security vulnerability (missing output forwarding), so it does not meet the security-impact threshold; could not verify the upstream default.

summary: Reviewed the assigned kubernetes-client/java snapshot (12.0.1-SNAPSHOT) with source tools plus the P1 relation index. I traced the hand-written modules (util, extended, spring, kubernetes custom classes, examples) and repeatedly checked trust boundaries: KubeConfig/ClientBuilder/ApiClient TLS + auth setup, Exec/Copy/Attach/PortForward web-socket paths, YAML/JSON parsing, informer/controller and leader-election logic, and dependency pins. TLS handling (ApiClient.applySslSettings, ClientBuilder.verifySSL wiring, SSLUtils keystore/CA loading) and the tar-extraction path handling in Copy are internally consistent and contain explicit mitigations. The strongest single issue I can support from source is unsafe SnakeYAML deserialization in the library's YAML entry points: io.kubernetes.client.util.Yaml uses a CustomConstructor extending org.yaml.snakeyaml.constructor.Constructor, and io.kubernetes.client.util.generic.dynamic.Dynamics uses the raw `new Yaml()`, while the root POM pins snakeyaml 1.28 (< 2.0, the version where arbitrary class instantiation via `!!` tags was restricted). Public APIs load(Reader/String/File), loadAs, loadAll and newFromYaml/fromYamlToJson feed caller-supplied YAML into that constructor, so a consuming application that parses untrusted manifests can be driven to instantiate attacker-chosen classes (CVE-2022-1471 class of RCE) in the client process. KubeConfig correctly uses SafeConstructor, which shows the safer alternative exists but is not applied to the manifest-parsing APIs. I submit this as the one candidate; the other plausible leads (Copy shell concatenation, FilePersister permissions, etc.) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed because their attacker model or impact is weaker or arguably by design.
